newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli union chief vows to fight economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Israeli union chief vows to fight economic reforms.

text.p: The head of the Israeli labour union federation warned on Thursday that unions would fight the government's plans to implement structural reforms but he stopped short of threatening a general strike.

"I think the programme to increase competition is a programme for increasing unemployment in Israel, attacking workers rights in almost every sector," Amir Peretz, secretary-general of the Histadrut labour federation, told reporters before a meeting with Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman.
Peretz did not say there would be a general strike but added "this is a possibility at some future date."
Responding, Neeman said "there is no need for fears from the work force. Growth will bring more jobs."

The meeting follows cabinet approval on Wednesday night of 100 structural reforms as part of an effort to revive Israel's flagging economic growth. The reforms include privatisation, capital market and foreign currency liberalisation, and sectoral deregulation.
At the same meeting, the cabinet also approved a Treasury plan to cut 2.3 billion shekels from 1998's planned 164.4 billion shekel budget and set next year's inflation target at seven to 10 percent.
Peretz accused the government of attempting to alter existing agreements on pension and provident funds and unemployment benefits.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel, meanwhile, criticised the cabinet's approval of the 1998 inflation target.
"Fixing the target at this level, which is identical to the 1997 target, does not reflect sufficient progress towards reducing inflation," Frenkel said in a statement.
He expressed support for the structural changes and the cabinet's decision to keep the budget deficit ceiling at 2.4 percent of gross domestic product as originally targeted.
Frenkel had reportedly been urging the government to reduce next year's inflation target to six to nine percent.
